pages.title: Welcome to the Animal Kingdom
bulletPoints: Earth is home to millions of amazing animals living on land, in deep blue oceans, and high in the sky.
Scientists divide animals into two big groups: Vertebrates (with backbones) and Invertebrates (without backbones).
From giant blue whales singing in the Pacific to tiny ladybugs in our garden, every creature has a special role.
Field prompt: Look outside your window and count how many different animals and birds you can spot today!

pages.title: Marvelous Mammals: Fur & Warm Hearts
bulletPoints: Warm-blooded wonders: Mammals can regulate their own body temperature whether in freezing snow or hot deserts.
Soft fur and hair: Shields mammal skin from thorns, keeps them warm, and provides camouflage.
Mothers nurse their babies with nutritious milk, teaching them how to find food and stay safe.
Examples: Friendly dogs, playful kittens, wild tigers, giant African elephants, and ocean dolphins!

pages.title: Birds: Masters of the Blue Sky
bulletPoints: Feathers for flight: Lightweight contour feathers create smooth aerodynamic wings.
Down feathers: Fluffy, soft feathers close to the skin trap warmth during cold nights.
Hollow bones: Bird skeletons are filled with tiny air pockets, making them light enough to soar effortlessly.
Beaks and claws: Eagles have curved talons for catching fish; hummingbirds have long straw-like beaks for sweet nectar.

pages.title: Underwater Wonders: The World of Fish
bulletPoints: Breathing with gills: Fish absorb life-giving dissolved oxygen directly from water currents.
Fins and tails: Pectoral fins help fish steer and balance; powerful caudal tails propel them forward.
Shimmering scales: Smooth, slippery overlapping scales protect fish bodies and reduce water drag.
Freshwater vs Saltwater: Goldfish and trout swim in cool rivers; clownfish and manta rays explore coral reefs.

pages.title: Reptiles: Cold-Blooded Sun Lovers
bulletPoints: Tough scaly skin: Waterproof scales stop reptiles from drying out in hot, sunbaked environments.
Cold-blooded nature: Reptiles cannot make their own body heat; they bask on warm rocks to gain energy.
Leathery shelled eggs: Turtles and crocodiles lay protective leathery eggs on warm sandy riverbanks.
Meet the reptiles: Gentle green sea turtles, colorful chameleons with 360-degree eyes, and desert geckos.

pages.title: Amphibians: The Double-Life Water Explorers
bulletPoints: Double life: Amphibians hatch in clean freshwater and transform into land-dwelling creatures as they grow.
Breathing through skin: Frogs can drink water and breathe air directly through their smooth, moist skin.
Tadpole metamorphosis: Swimming tadpoles with tails grow strong jumping legs and lose their tails to become frogs.
Examples: Spotted green tree frogs, woodland salamanders, and gentle garden toads catching insects.

pages.title: Creepy Crawlies: The Invertebrate Superstars
bulletPoints: Invertebrates have no backbone: They make up over 95 percent of all animal species on planet Earth!
Exoskeletons: Crabs, beetles, and lobsters wear hard protective suits of armor on the outside of their bodies.
Soft-bodied wonders: Earthworms enrich garden soil; ocean octopuses use suction cups and squirt dark ink to escape.
Jellyfish and sea anemones: Graceful floating ocean bells that drift with rhythmic ocean tides.

pages.title: Insects: Six-Legged Garden Wonders
bulletPoints: Three body parts: Head, thorax, and abdomen with two sensitive antennae for smelling flowers.
Six walking legs: Grasshoppers jump high with springy hind legs; honeybees carry pollen baskets on their knees.
Metamorphosis: A caterpillar hatches from an egg, wraps itself into a cozy chrysalis, and emerges as a butterfly!
Super strength: Ants can lift pebbles and leaves weighing fifty times their own tiny body weight.

pages.title: Animal Homes & Cozy Shelters
bulletPoints: Birds weave intricate nests from dried grass, twigs, and spider silk high in tall leafy branches.
Beavers build incredible wooden lodges in rushing streams with secret underwater entrance tunnels.
Prairie dogs dig vast underground tunnel cities called towns, complete with guard posts and nursery rooms.
Honeybees engineer perfect six-sided hexagonal wax combs to store golden honey and nurture baby bee larvae.

pages.title: Herbivores: The Gentle Plant Munchers
bulletPoints: Herbivores eat only plants, sweet fruits, green leaves, tree bark, and tender field grass.
Flat grinding teeth: Cows, sheep, and horses have broad molars to chew tough plant fibers into smooth paste.
Long necks: Tall giraffes reach high into thorny acacia treetops to pluck the sweetest young leaves.
Gentle giants: Giant pandas spend twelve hours every day happily crunching on crisp green bamboo stalks.

pages.title: Carnivores: The Skilled Hunters
bulletPoints: Carnivores eat meat and hunt for their nourishment in wild savannahs, arctic ice, and dark forests.
Sharp canine teeth: Lions and wolves have pointed fangs designed to grasp food firmly.
Binocular vision: Forward-facing eyes allow hunters to judge distances and leap with pinpoint accuracy.
Keen senses: Owls fly completely silently through the night air and hear a mouse scurrying under fallen leaves.

pages.title: Omnivores: Eating Both Plants & Meat
bulletPoints: Omnivores enjoy the best of both worlds: Eating berries, nuts, roots, fish, and insects.
Versatile teeth: Combining sharp front teeth for slicing with flat back molars for crushing seeds.
Bears feast on summer blackberries, dig up wild roots, and splash into rivers to catch leaping salmon.
Raccoons, crows, and garden badgers are famous for their clever problem-solving curiosity.

pages.title: Masters of Camouflage: The Art of Hiding
bulletPoints: Stick insects look exactly like brown twigs and sway gently in the breeze to trick hungry birds.
Arctic foxes turn snowy white in freezing winter and earthy brown in summer to blend with gravel.
Cuttlefish can change their skin color, pattern, and bumpy texture in a split second to vanish into reef rock.
Striped tigers blend seamlessly into tall dry golden grasslands under dappled forest sunlight.

pages.title: Animal Super Senses
bulletPoints: Eagle eyes: An eagle can spot a tiny scampering field mouse from over three kilometers up in the clouds.
Bat echolocation: Bats emit high-pitched clicking sounds and listen to the bouncing echoes to map the dark.
Elephant low rumble: Elephants communicate with secret seismic infrasound vibrations that travel miles through the earth.
Dog super snout: A bloodhound's sense of smell is up to 100,000 times more sensitive than human noses!

pages.title: The Great Migration: Epic Journeys
bulletPoints: Monarch butterflies flutter over 4,000 kilometers from cool Canadian forests all the way to warm Mexican fir groves.
Arctic Terns fly from the North Pole to the South Pole and back every single year, chasing endless sunshine.
Millions of wildebeest and zebras march across African plains crossing the Mara River following seasonal rains.
Humpback whales travel from icy polar feeding grounds to warm tropical bays to nurse newborn whale calves.

pages.title: Cold Polar Life: Penguins & Polar Bears
bulletPoints: Emperor Penguins huddle tightly together against Antarctic blizzards, taking turns standing in the warm center.
Blubber: A thick layer of insulating fat under the skin keeps seals and walruses toasty in freezing seawater.
Polar bears have black skin under their translucent fur to absorb every bit of warm solar heat.
Padded snowshoe paws: Wide furry paws stop polar bears from slipping on slick arctic pack ice.

pages.title: Hot Desert Survivors
bulletPoints: Camels store energy-rich fat in their humps and can walk for days across dry sandy dunes without water.
Long eyelashes and closing nostrils keep blowing desert sand out of camel eyes and noses.
Fennec foxes have giant radar-dish ears that radiate excess body heat away into the cool evening breeze.
Kangaroo rats never need to drink water: They get all the moisture they need from dry desert seeds!

pages.title: Nocturnal Animals: Life After Sunset
bulletPoints: Owls have giant round eyes packed with light-sensitive rod cells to see clearly under the silver moon.
Fireflies flash rhythmic yellow-green light pulses from their glowing abdomens to signal friendly firefly mates.
Hedgehogs snuffle through nighttime garden hedges hunting for crunchy slugs and earthworms.
Night active benefits: Avoiding the scorching daytime heat and finding food when predators are fast asleep.

pages.title: The Web of Life: Nature's Balance
bulletPoints: Ecosystem: A vibrant community where every plant, herbivore, predator, and decomposer depends on each other.
Producers: Green plants make food using warm golden sunlight.
Primary and secondary consumers: Energy flows from grass to zebra to lion in a harmonious circle of life.
Decomposers: Earthworms, mushrooms, and soil beetles recycle fallen autumn leaves into rich, fertile earth.

pages.title: Protecting Our Animal Friends
bulletPoints: Endangered species: Animals like snow leopards, rhinos, and sea turtles need our love and protection.
Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks create safe natural forests where animals roam wild and free.
Small kindnesses: Putting out clean water bowls for birds in summer and keeping plastic out of oceans.
Earth promise: Respect all living creatures, preserve their wild habitats, and celebrate wildlife diversity!
